a.t: Text A: The Night Market App
a.x: When Farah's family stall at the Taman Melati night market lost customers to food delivery apps, she decided to fight back with technology. With help from her computer science teacher, she built a simple website that showed the stall's menu, prices and live waiting time. Customers could order in advance and collect their food without queuing. At first, only a few regulars used it. Farah then printed a QR code on the stall's banner and offered a free drink for every fifth online order. Within two months, online orders made up almost half of the stall's sales. Farah admits the project was exhausting: she often coded after midnight and had to fix bugs before the market opened. However, she says the hardest part was persuading her father, who believed that 'good food sells itself'. He changed his mind when he saw the queue disappear and the profits rise.

c.x: Scientists recommend that teenagers sleep between eight and ten hours a night, yet surveys show that most get far less. One reason is biological: during puberty, the body releases the sleep hormone melatonin later in the evening, so teenagers naturally feel awake at night. Another reason is the glow of phone screens, which can delay sleep even further. Lack of sleep affects memory, mood and even the immune system. Some schools abroad have experimented with later start times, and early results show better attendance and fewer car accidents among teenage drivers. Critics argue that later starts would disrupt parents' work schedules and after-school activities. Most experts agree, however, that simple habits such as switching off devices an hour before bed can make a real difference.

a.x: When Farah's family stall at the Taman Melati night market lost customers to food delivery apps, she decided to fight back with technology. With help from her computer science teacher, she built a simple website that showed the stall's menu, prices and live waiting time. c.x: Scientists recommend that teenagers sleep between eight and ten hours a night, yet surveys show that most get far less. One reason is biological: during puberty, the body releases the sleep hormone melatonin later in the evening, so teenagers naturally feel awake at night. Another reason is the glow of phone screens, which can delay sleep even further. Lack of sleep affects memory, mood and even the immune system. Some schools abroad have experimented with later start times, and early results show better attendance and fewer car accidents among teenage drivers. Critics argue that later starts would disrupt parents' work schedules and after-school activities. Most experts agree, however, that simple habits such as switching off devices an hour before bed can make a real difference.
